hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever eaten a meal that tasted better because of when, or who, you ate it with?
options: then you already know the spice. listen.
then this story is yours. listen.
that’s what the emperor thought. listen.

steps.line: The Talmud tells this. A Roman emperor asked Rabbi Yehoshua, “Why does the food you eat on Shabbat smell so wonderful?”
The rabbi smiled. “We have a spice,” he said, “and its name is Shabbat. We put it in the food, and that’s the smell.”

steps.q: The emperor wants the spice. What does the rabbi tell him?
o: “It only works for those who keep Shabbat.”
“It only works on a Friday night.”
“It only works if cooked before sundown.”
steps.why: You can’t buy it; you have to stop. Shabbat 119a names the sage as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah, who spars with the emperor, often taken as Hadrian, all through Jewish legend.

steps.line: “For anyone who keeps Shabbat,” said Rabbi Yehoshua, “it works. For anyone who doesn’t keep Shabbat, it doesn’t.”

steps.q: In a midrash, Rabbi Judah serves his friend the emperor Antoninus cold food on Shabbat and hot food on a weekday. Which does he like better?
steps.why: Genesis Rabbah 11:4: the cold Shabbat dishes won (no cooking on Shabbat). The weekday food lacked one spice, Rabbi told him: Shabbat.

steps.line: The Torah says that on the seventh day God finished the work, and rested. Then God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy.

steps.q: The rabbis list 39 kinds of work stopped on Shabbat. Where did they find the list?
o: The jobs of a farmer’s year
The labours of slaves in Egypt
The work of building the Tabernacle
steps.why: The Mishnah lists the 39 (Shabbat 7:2), and the Talmud traces them to building the Tabernacle, God’s dwelling in the desert. The work that made a holy place stops, to keep a holy time.

steps.line: Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday night. Orthodox Jews don’t drive, cook or use phones. Many other Jews keep it their own way, with candles, a meal and rest.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Shabbat starts Friday at sunset, not at midnight or dawn. Why?
o: Candles must be lit after dark
In Genesis, each day starts at evening
Work used to end at sunset
steps.why: “And there was evening, and there was morning, one day.” So every Jewish day, and every holiday, begins at sundown. (Candles are lit just before.)

say: here’s what i love. the torah says god finished the work on the seventh day. the rabbis asked: wasn’t it done on the sixth? one answer: the world still lacked one thing, rest. so rest was created on the seventh day, and only then was the world finished.
and the first thing the torah calls holy isn’t a mountain or a temple. it’s a day. a stretch of time.

steps.q: If the world wasn’t finished until rest was created, what does that say about stopping?
o: Stopping is part of the work being complete
Stopping is just a reward for working hard
steps.why: A week without rest isn’t finished. The stopping is part of the making.

today.say: this friday, or any day, pick one hour to stop on purpose: no work, no errands, maybe a candle and a slow meal. keep it in your own way. that’s where the spice comes from.
options: one hour of rest. you’ll taste it.
a meal kept on purpose. that’s the spice.

tomorrow.title: Two pockets.
tomorrow.line: a rabbi tells his students to carry two slips of paper, one in each pocket. the trick is knowing which one to reach for.
